Albuquerque housing market context

Albuquerque is Bernalillo County's seat and New Mexico's largest city, with 564,559 residents counted in 2020 and a 2025 estimate of 556,588. The metro area holds about 955,000 people. The city runs from roughly 4,900 feet near the Rio Grande to more than 6,700 feet in the foothills around Sandia Heights, and that spread shows up in houses: a valley address and a foothill address a few miles apart can differ in weather, views and insurance questions.

Federal research, defense, higher education and health care anchor local employment. Sandia National Laboratories and Kirtland Air Force Base are the big federal names, and the University of New Mexico is the largest university in the state. Those jobs bring relocations, so Albuquerque has owners who must leave quickly and buyers who need to move in just as fast.

Property tax due dates in Bernalillo County

Bernalillo County splits the yearly bill into two installments. The first half is due November 10 and late fees begin December 10. The second half is due April 10 and turns delinquent after May 10. For the current 2026 bills, the second half is due April 10, 2027, and it becomes delinquent if unpaid by May 10, 2027.

Selling with a tax balance

If you owe tax on the house, you can still sell it. Ask the Treasurer's office or the title company for a payoff figure close to the signing date, so you are not guessing about late fees. Any unpaid amount comes off your proceeds along with a mortgage payoff or a recorded lien. Collect your latest bill and a record of past payments so the title company can reconcile them without delay.

Casitas, guest houses and city zoning

Land use in Albuquerque is governed by the Integrated Development Ordinance, which the City Council updated in 2025. The Planning Department takes questions at 505-924-3860.

Older properties often include an accessory dwelling unit, which the city calls a casita. The city's page allows one casita per lot in R-A and R-1 zones. If you have a guest house or a converted garage, confirm it was built with a permit and counts as a legal unit before advertising it as an extra bedroom or a rental.

A buyer using a loan may ask for unpermitted space to be legalized. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands. Properties near one of the city's more than 160 historic sites may face extra review, so ask the city before planning exterior work.

Sun, snow and what inspectors check

Albuquerque has a cold semi-arid climate. Annual precipitation is under half of evaporation, and no month averages below freezing. The Sandia Mountains cast a rain shadow over much of the city.

  • Roofs and stucco wear from strong sun more than from rain.
  • Evaporative cooling and heating equipment age fast under year-round use.
  • Foothill and East Mountain homes see more snow than the valley, which can affect roofs and access roads.

None of this blocks a sale, but an inspector will go through the roof, cooling unit and stucco, and each can turn into a repair request. A cash purchase avoids that negotiation.

Commutes, rail and the airport

The Albuquerque International Sunport is about 3 miles southeast of the central business district. The Rail Runner Express began service in July 2006 and links Santa Fe, Sandoval, Bernalillo and Valencia Counties with thirteen stops, three of them in Albuquerque. Buyers ask about commute and airport access, so mention them in a listing.

If you already live in another state, those same facts are a reason to favor a sale that needs no trips back for showings or repairs.

Selling from out of state

Many Albuquerque sellers are not in town. Federal and university jobs move people around, and an owner who has relocated is paying for a house they cannot watch. Each month of delay means another tax installment, utilities and upkeep on an empty building.

A sale that needs few showings helps. Pick one local contact for the walkthrough, send the title company a power of attorney or signed documents as it directs, and confirm the date for the keys. Ask the closing agent how proceeds will reach you, by wire or by check.

Valley and foothill houses compared

Buyers read the two areas differently. In the valley near the river and bosque, ask about drainage and lot grading. In the foothills and the East Mountain, ask about snow load on the roof, access roads in winter and the insurance cost. Sellers who can answer those questions in a short note tend to field fewer surprises at the inspection stage.

An older house in either area deserves a quick look at the stucco, the roofline and the cooling unit before any buyer arrives. Fixing a small crack costs less than a negotiation credit, though a cash buyer will price what they see and skip the haggling.

Your options for selling a house in Albuquerque

The choice usually comes down to how much time, repair money and certainty you have.

  • Traditional listing: the most buyers see it, though commission, repair requests, an appraisal and loan approval all stand between you and the closing.
  • For sale by owner: you save the commission but carry the marketing, showings and paperwork.
  • Cash sale to us: an as-is purchase with no commission, no repair requests, and a closing date set around you.

We do not promise a price. An offer reflects condition, location and needed repairs, and it will usually sit below a fully renovated retail sale. Cash can be simpler when you have back taxes, a probate property, a tenant you want to hand over, or a house needing work you cannot afford.

Questions to ask before you pick a route

Before choosing, put three questions to yourself. How soon must the money arrive? Can you pay for a roof, cooling or stucco repair out of pocket? Would you rather hold showings for weeks or take one visit and an answer? Your replies point toward a listing, a for-sale-by-owner attempt or a direct cash sale. None is wrong. The best match is the one that suits your calendar and your budget for repairs.

From offer to closing

Once you accept an offer, a title company opens the file. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage, lien or tax from your proceeds, and records the deed. Bring the deed or probate paperwork, your latest tax bill, any loan statement and permit records for a casita or other additions. Ask for the offer in writing and confirm who pays each closing cost before you sign.

An as-is sale means no repair list from the buyer. You still owe honest answers about what you know of the roof, cooling and any unpermitted space.

Who collects property tax in Albuquerque?

The Bernalillo County Treasurer bills and collects it, and the County Assessor sets the value. The city sends no separate bill.

When are Bernalillo County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10 with late fees starting December 10. The second half is due April 10 and turns delinquent after May 10.

Can I sell an Albuquerque house with a casita or guest house?

Yes. Confirm first that it was permitted, since the city allows one casita per lot in R-A and R-1 zones. A cash buyer can take the property as-is.

Do I have to make repairs before a cash sale in Albuquerque?

No. A cash purchase is as-is, so roof, cooling and stucco problems do not need to be fixed first.

Does elevation matter when selling in Albuquerque?

It can. The city ranges from about 4,900 feet by the river to over 6,700 feet in the foothills, so snow, views and insurance questions vary by neighborhood.

Las Cruces housing market context

Second in size among New Mexico cities, Las Cruces counted 111,385 residents in 2020 and serves as the seat of Doña Ana County. The Rio Grande runs through the Mesilla Valley here, 225 miles south of Albuquerque and 42 miles northwest of El Paso, at about 3,908 feet. Shopping has moved to the east side while the historic center stays near Main Street, so buyers shopping east of town and buyers wanting a downtown feel are often different people.

White Sands Missile Range and the White Sands Test Facility make the federal government the top employer, followed by New Mexico State University, the schools, the city and the hospitals. That mix of jobs brings a wide pool of buyers, and retirees from other states have added to growth.

Heat, monsoon storms and arroyos

Las Cruces has a cool desert climate. Rain is very light from October to June, then heavy afternoon thunderstorms arrive in late summer. The average year brings light freezes on 69 nights, spring wind that can raise blowing dust, and summer stretches above 100 degrees. The record high is 110 degrees.

Dry streams called arroyos cut across the uplands on both sides of the valley and run after hard storms. Even with little rain overall, a house beside an arroyo or on a low lot can see water in monsoon season. Look up the address on the FEMA flood map and have your insurance history at hand.

  • Roof condition and drainage after monsoon rain
  • Cooling systems that have run through summers above 100 degrees
  • Stucco cracks and window seals worn by sun and wind
  • Dust and filter condition in the HVAC system

Vacant and abandoned property registration

An owner whose building stays empty a long time has to register it with the city every year and pay a fee that rises annually. The rule reaches buildings, or parts of them, with no lawful occupancy or operation for two years running. New properties get a 24-month break after the certificate of occupancy.

Owners can apply for exemptions, including for construction or rehabilitation, foreclosure redemption periods, secured properties in probate or ownership litigation, and active sale or lease marketing that meets pricing and marketing requirements. An exemption needs city approval, lasts 12 months and can be renewed once. Appeal a final vacancy assessment in writing to the Community Development Director within 30 days. Questions go to Vacancy@LasCruces.gov or 575-541-2299.

When a house you inherited has been empty nearly two years, ask the city how the registration and fee apply to you before you list or sign anything.

Nuisance properties and code enforcement

Property upkeep follows the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, with minimum standards for use, occupancy and maintenance of residential, non-residential, vacant and boarded buildings. A Nuisance Abatement Team drawn from Code Enforcement, Community Development, Fire, Legal, Police and other departments works on problem properties.

Residents report weeds and other code issues through dispatch at 575-526-0975 or an online non-emergency portal, and a public map shows properties on the nuisance list. A condemned property is one judged unfit for occupancy. Condemnation does not mean the city is taking or tearing down the building, and owners can contact Community Development about abatement options and permits for repair or demolition.

A house on that list, or one a neighbor has complained about, should be dealt with before you sell. Cash buyers can accept open code issues, but the title company needs to hear about liens or fines.

Doña Ana County property tax dates and penalties

The county mails bills by November 1. November 10 is the due date for the first half, with delinquency after December 10, and April 10 is the date for the second, with delinquency after May 10. Late balances gather 1 percent interest monthly plus a 1 percent penalty for up to five months, with a $5 minimum, and neither can be waived once it accrues.

A parcel carrying three or more delinquent years can go to a state auction unless every year is paid, so settle back taxes before or at closing.

Protests, exemptions and proration

  • Proration: the county does not split a bill between owners. Whoever is the owner of record on January 1 owes that year, and a lien attaches if it is unpaid no matter who owns the house later. The two sides normally divide the cost at the title company.
  • Valuation protest: tell the Assessor within 30 days after the Notice of Value arrives, usually in April. If you miss that window, the remaining route is a refund claim in District Court, after paying by December 10 and filing by January 10.
  • Exemptions: the state offers no homestead exemption. A head of family exemption exists, and so does a valuation freeze for owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, with modified gross income under $35,000.
  • Mobile homes: title cannot transfer until the Assessor issues a property tax release, paid in cash, by cashier's check or by money order.

Preparing a vacant or inherited house

Check three things first: how long the house has stood empty, whether any city notice has been posted, and who has legal authority to sign. Photograph the condition, secure doors and windows, and keep utilities on if the weather could damage plumbing. These steps protect the value of the house while you decide on a route and keep the closing on schedule once you have a buyer.

Roads, utilities and closing-day tasks

Interstate 10 and Interstate 25 meet here, and Las Cruces is the southern end of I-25. Las Cruces International Airport has service to Albuquerque on Advanced Air. The city provides water, sewer, natural gas and solid waste service, and El Paso Electric supplies power. Final bills and meter readings are a closing-day task, so arrange them with the buyer in advance.

Which sale route fits

Choices are an agent listing, a direct sale or a cash offer. For a house in good shape, a listing may get the strongest price. Cash makes sense when the house is vacant and facing the registry fee, in probate, rented to a difficult tenant, or in need of more repair than you can pay for.

Frequently asked questions

When are Doña Ana County property taxes due?

Mailing goes out by November 1. First-half tax is due November 10, delinquent after December 10; second-half tax is due April 10, delinquent after May 10.

Do I need to register a vacant house in Las Cruces?

Possibly. A building with no lawful occupancy or operation for two straight years may fall under the city ordinance and need yearly registration, with a residential fee that begins at $500. Write to Vacancy@LasCruces.gov.

Can I get an exemption from the vacancy fee if I am selling?

Active marketing for sale or lease can qualify if it meets the city's pricing and marketing rules. The exemption needs city approval and lasts 12 months.

Can I protest my Las Cruces property valuation?

Yes, within 30 days of the Notice of Value, usually in April, through the county Assessor. After a missed deadline, pay by December 10 and file a refund claim in District Court by January 10.

What happens if the house has code violations?

Code Enforcement and the Nuisance Abatement Team handle them. You can still sell, though any fine or lien gets settled at closing.

Rio Rancho and the two-county question

Rio Rancho spreads across the Albuquerque Basin, nearly all of it in Sandoval County and a small northern piece in Bernalillo County. With 114,419 people at the 2025 estimate (104,046 in 2020) it is the biggest city in Sandoval County. It covers about 103.7 square miles at around 5,509 feet.

Which county sends your tax bill decides who you call. A property in the Bernalillo piece answers to a different assessor and treasurer than the rest of town, so read your latest bill first and then pick up the phone.

A planned community with a mix of ages

The city started as a land-sales project: in 1961 AMREP bought about 55,000 acres and platted Rio Rancho Estates, and families began moving in during the early 1960s. Incorporation came in 1981, the same year Intel opened a plant. Between 1970 and 1980 the population grew ten-fold, and it has kept rising.

The result is a patchwork. An older house can sit beside much newer ones, which is why buyers ask how old the roof and major systems are. After the 2008 housing collapse, foreclosures climbed here, and the city later passed an abandoned residential property registration ordinance, described below.

Intel leads local employment, ahead of the school district and a hospital. Its local headcount has dropped, so demand for houses can move with that company's news. Retail, services and government make up the remainder.

Dry climate and inspections

Annual precipitation is only about 8.90 inches. Rio Rancho lies in the rain shadow of the Sandia Mountains on one side and the Continental Divide on the other, and the higher west side picks up a little more rain and snow than the denser east side.

A dry climate still leaves work for an inspector. Expect questions about the roof, water drainage near the foundation and the exterior finish. With an investor or cash buyer those items are priced into the offer, so you can skip the repairs.

Permits, short-term rentals and abandoned homes

Permits. Construction permits and inspections come from the city's Building Division. Before starting a home project, phone 505-891-5005 to find out if a permit applies. The 2021 International Residential Code is among the governing codes. Work a former owner did without a permit can come up in a sale, so collect whatever records you hold.

Short-term rentals. A permit has been required since July 1, 2025 to operate, rent, offer or advertise a short-term rental, meaning a stay under 30 days in a single-family residence. A 5% Lodgers' Tax applies and Development Services may fine up to $500 per day. If the house was used this way, a new owner needs their own permit, so tell the buyer early.

Abandoned property. In December 2011 the Governing Body approved an Abandoned Residential Property Registration ordinance. For a house left empty after an owner dies or moves away, read it on the Code Enforcement pages.

Sandoval County property tax calendar

Deeds, back taxes and closing

The assessor changes the owner only after a deed is recorded with the county clerk, and a title company records it for you at closing. Most of the city is in Rio Rancho Public Schools. Parts lie in Jemez Valley Public Schools, and much of the Bernalillo County section is zoned to Albuquerque Public Schools. Many buyers begin with the district line, so verify yours before you describe the house.

ABQ RIDE route 251 links Rio Rancho with the Rail Runner station at Journal Center, and Rio Metro commuter buses run toward the US 550 station. Albuquerque lies right to the south, so driving is the usual commute.

Ways to sell a Rio Rancho house

Owners have three paths, which differ in cost, time and effort.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers, with showings, inspections and repair requests along the way.
  • Selling it yourself: avoids a commission, but marketing, paperwork and negotiation are yours.
  • Cash offer: the buyer takes the house as it stands, so repairs and cleaning drop off your list. Get the offer in writing and compare it with your likely net on the other routes.

Cash is worth a look when the house was inherited, payments have fallen behind, tenants live in it, or the repair list is longer than your budget. Whatever you choose, keep every offer and every message about it in writing.

Steps before you accept an offer

Start by learning which county bills you, then pull the latest tax statement. Collect permit records, plus any short-term rental permit paperwork if the house was rented that way. Decide whether you are willing to wait for a buyer who needs a loan or would rather get a quick close. Finally, choose a title company and ask ahead of time how tax, liens and closing costs will be split.

If the house is empty, check for open notices from Code Enforcement. Clearing a notice, or telling the buyer about it, avoids a late surprise at the table.

Handling older houses in a newer city

Because the city grew in waves, sellers of older homes face a different set of questions than owners on newer streets. Roofs, water heaters and cooling equipment from the early decades are the usual focus. You do not need to hide age; you do need to answer questions about it. Write down when major work was done and keep the receipts. Buyers who plan to pay cash will use that history to set a price they can stand behind. A tidy folder of dates and receipts also makes a closing day less stressful, since the title company can answer its own questions without calling you repeatedly.

Mostly Sandoval County, with a small northern section in Bernalillo County. Your tax bill shows which assessor and treasurer handle your property.

Bills are mailed by November 1. Pay the first half by November 10 (delinquent after December 10) and the second half by April 10 (delinquent after May 10).

Do I need a permit to run a short-term rental in Rio Rancho?

Yes. A permit has been required since July 1, 2025 to operate, rent or advertise one, along with a 5% Lodgers' Tax. Fines can reach $500 per day.

Winter, snow and wildfire risk

A typical year brings 12.79 inches of precipitation and 20.2 inches of snow. The 24-hour average temperature climbs from 30.3 degrees in December to 70.1 in July, which makes heating a real expense for much of the year.

A buyer who wants to change a front facade, windows or walls inside a district may need review first.

If your house sits in a district, tell any buyer early, and ask the Historic Preservation Division what is on file for the address. Questions go to historicpreservation@santafenm.gov and submittals to hpdsubmittal@santafenm.gov, so you can ask in writing what has been approved or filed.

Wind never really stops in Clovis, a dry plains town on the southern edge of Tornado Alley. Gusts often pass 30 miles per hour and the average speed is about 12 across open, flat ground. Severe thunderstorms arrive in spring, heavy rain shows up on summer evenings, and snow lingers for several weeks in January and February.

The town has almost no storm runoff system, so snowmelt and heavy rain can cause minor street flooding. A low lot or a garage floor level with the street will draw questions.
